title: DEL‐1 is an Endogenous Senolytic Protein that Inhibits Senescence‐Associated Bone Loss

sections.abstract: Accumulation of senescent cells in the bone microenvironment, including bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells (BM‐MSCs), contributes to aging‐related bone degeneration. Developmental endothelial locus‐1 (DEL‐1), the expression of which declines with old age is herein described as an endogenous secreted senolytic protein. DEL‐1 promotes apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSCs via a β3 integrin/CD73/adenosine/p38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK)/B‐cell lymphoma‐2 (BCL‐2) pathway, thereby leading to their clearance by macrophages. DEL‐1‐deficiency displays increased abundance of β3 integrin‐rich CD73 + senescent BM‐MSCs and higher chemotherapy‐induced or aging‐related senescence‐associated bone loss. Conversely, mice with endothelial‐specific overexpression of DEL‐1 (EC‐Del1) have decreased numbers of senescent BM‐MSCs and diminish senescence‐associated bone loss. CD73‐deficiency reverses the reduction in senescent BM‐MSC numbers in EC‐Del1 mice. Administration of DEL‐1 (or a DEL‐1‐inducing macrolide) causes a reduction in senescence markers and reverses aging‐related periodontitis. Therefore, DEL‐1 may be harnessed as an endogenous senolytic to prevent senescent cell buildup and senescence‐associated bone loss.
sections.introduction:
Cellular senescence is a complex biological process associated with aging, characterized by irreversible cell‐cycle arrest in response to various stress stimuli, including DNA damage, telomere shortening, oncogenic mutations, metabolic and mitochondrial dysfunction, as well as inflammation. [ 1 , 2 ] Senescent cells display several distinctive features, such as, an enlarged and flattened cell morphology, [ 3 ] enhanced senescence‐associated β‐galactosidase (SA‐β‐gal) activity, [ 4 ] increased expression of senescence markers ( e.g ., the cyclin‐dependent kinase inhibitors p16 [ 5 ] and p21 and the tumor‐suppressor p53 protein [ 6 ] ) along with a senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP). SASP is characterized by the release of high levels of pro‐inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and extracellular matrix‐degrading enzymes, which via paracrine effects can spread senescence in neighboring cells. [ 7 , 8 , 9 ]

Senescent cells can in principle be removed by immune‐mediated clearance via macrophage phagocytosis [ 10 , 11 ] or by killing via degranulation of natural killer cells. [ 12 , 13 ] However, senescent cells are generally resistant to macrophage phagocytosis or killing, in part due to elevated expression of the “don't eat me” signal CD47 on their surface. [ 14 ] Moreover, with advancing age, the mechanisms for the removal of senescent cells from the tissues become even more ineffective. [ 12 , 15 ] This aging‐related decline of the immune system's efficiency in removing senescent cells contributes to their accumulation within tissues, ultimately leading to impaired tissue function and age‐related pathologies. [ 12 , 15 ] Another factor contributing to the persistence of senescent cells involves the activation of specific pathways known as senescent cell anti‐apoptotic pathways (SCAPs). [ 16 ] For instance, increased expression of anti‐apoptotic proteins, such as B‐cell lymphoma‐2 (BCL‐2), enables senescent cells to resist apoptosis and thus persist in tissues during aging or chronic inflammation. [ 16 ] Senolytic treatment with BCL2‐family inhibitors, including ABT‐263 and ABT‐737, has been proven effective in eliminating senescent cells. [ 17 , 18 ]

Accumulation of senescent cells in the bone microenvironment has been linked to age‐related bone loss. [ 19 ] Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) in the bone marrow stroma are multipotent cells that can differentiate along the osteogenic lineage and facilitate bone regeneration. [ 20 ] However, in aging, the function of bone marrow MSCs is remarkably impaired. [ 20 , 21 ] For instance, the osteogenic differentiation potency of MSCs diminishes over time and, moreover, MSCs can undergo senescence as the bone ages. [ 22 ] Senescent MSCs suppress osteogenesis via paracrine effects [ 23 ] ; conversely, their removal can enhance the osteogenic activity and bone‐forming potential of healthy MSCs, thereby preventing age‐related bone loss. [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ]

Developmental endothelial locus‐1 (DEL‐1) is a multi‐functional protein secreted by various stromal cells that comprises three N ‐terminal epidermal growth factor (EGF)‐like repeats and two C ‐terminal discoidin I‐like domains 3 (hence also known as EDIL3). [ 28 ] Its second EGF‐like repeat (E2) contains an Arg‐Gly‐Asp (RGD) motif, which mediates binding to β3 integrins, while its discoidin I‐like domains interact with phosphatidylserine (PS). [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] In addition, DEL‐1 binds β2 integrins, thereby regulating neutrophil recruitment to inflammatory sites. [ 32 , 33 ] The ability of DEL‐1 to bind both αvβ3 integrin on macrophages and the “eat‐me” signal PS on apoptotic cells enables the interaction of apoptotic cells with macrophages, thereby promoting apoptotic cell phagocytosis (efferocytosis) and resolution of inflammation. [ 29 ] DEL‐1 also contributes to the regulation of myelopoiesis in the bone marrow [ 34 ] and stimulates osteogenic differentiation [ 35 ] via interaction with β3 integrins on hematopoietic stem cells and osteoprogenitors, respectively. By virtue of its anti‐inflammatory and pro‐resolving properties, DEL‐1 provides protection against various inflammation‐associated pathologies, including experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis as well as inflammatory bone loss in periodontitis and arthritis. [ 32 , 33 , 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 ] The expression of DEL‐1 in stromal cells (e.g., endothelial cells, perivascular stromal cells, and MSCs) helps maintain tissue homeostasis. [ 33 , 36 , 38 , 40 ] However, DEL‐1 expression declines severely with aging in both mice and humans and this aging‐related deficiency of DEL‐1 is associated with enhanced inflammation and disease susceptibility. [ 28 , 33 ]

In this study, we investigated whether DEL‐1 plays a role in the association between MSC senescence and bone loss during aging or after chemotherapy. By using chemotherapy‐induced and aging‐related senescence models along with multiple complementary genetic approaches, we demonstrated that DEL‐1 exhibits senolytic properties on senescent bone‐marrow derived MSCs (BM‐MSCs) in a β3 integrin‐dependent manner, thereby promoting their clearance by macrophages. The DEL‐1‐mediated senolytic activity mainly targeted ecto‐5′‐nucleotidase (CD73)‐expressing PDGFRα + Sca1 + (PαS) BM‐MSCs, which exhibited increased expression of β3 integrin compared to other subsets of BM‐MSCs. Whereas DEL‐1 overexpression in endothelial cells markedly reduced senescent BM‐MSC numbers and senescence‐associated bone loss, this activity was abrogated in the genetic absence of CD73. Mechanistically, the senolytic effect of DEL‐1 was dependent on a CD73/Adenosine/p38 mitogen‐activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK)/BCL‐2 pathway. Taken together, we demonstrated for the first time that DEL‐1 is an endogenously expressed senolytic protein in the bone marrow niche that mediates senescent cell clearance and prevents senescence‐associated bone loss.
sections.results:
The accumulation of senescent MSCs in aged tissues has been implicated in age‐related bone loss pathologies including osteoarthritis [ 41 ] and osteoporosis, [ 27 ] whereas clearance of senescent cells is essential for inflammation resolution and tissue regeneration. [ 24 , 27 ] We previously demonstrated that full‐length DEL‐1 ( i.e ., containing both the N ‐terminal EGF‐like repeats and the C ‐terminal discoidin‐like domains) acts as a molecular bridge that promotes macrophage phagocytosis of apoptotic neutrophils, thereby promoting inflammation resolution. [ 29 ] This finding prompted us to investigate whether DEL‐1 could also contribute to macrophage clearance of senescent BM‐MSCs. BM‐MSC senescence was induced by exposure to an oxidative stressor, H 2 O 2 . The senescent state of the cells was confirmed by real‐time quantitative PCR (qPCR) for p16 and p21 expression (Figure S1A , Supporting Information), immunocytochemistry (SA‐β‐gal staining using X‐gal chromogenic substrate) and by flow cytometric analysis (using the fluorescent β‐galactosidase substrate C 12 FDG) ( Figure 1 A ); the latter analysis showed that BM‐MSCs became fully senescent at day 8 following H 2 O 2 treatment (Figure 1A , right). To explore whether DEL‐1 can promote macrophage phagocytosis of senescent BM‐MSCs, we first conducted an in vitro macrophage phagocytosis assay by co‐culturing bone marrow‐derived macrophages with H 2 O 2 ‐induced senescent BM‐MSCs pre‐stained with a pH‐sensitive dye, CypHer5E, in the presence of recombinant DEL‐1 (expressed as an Fc‐fusion protein; DEL‐1‐Fc) or Fc control. The percentage of phagocytic (CypHer5E + ) macrophages in total CD45 + F4/80 + macrophages was significantly increased in the presence of DEL‐1‐Fc as compared to Fc control treatment (Figure 1B ). To determine the in vivo relevance of this observation, we performed thioglycolate (TG)‐induced peritonitis, which is conducive for investigating quantitative aspects of macrophage phagocytosis. [ 42 ] To this end, we isolated BM‐MSCs from human ubiquitin C promoter‐green fluorescent protein (UBC‐GFP) mice and induced senescence by H 2 O 2 , as confirmed by significantly elevated p16 and p21 expression (Figure S1B , Supporting Information). At 72 h after TG injection, cultured GFP‐expressing CypHer5E + senescent BM‐MSCs were administered together with DEL‐1‐Fc or Fc control into naive wild‐type (WT) mice and peritoneal macrophage phagocytic activity was assessed 3 h later by flow cytometry (Figure 1C ). Mice that received senescent GFP + BM‐MSCs with DEL‐1‐Fc displayed a higher percentage of CypHer5E + peritoneal macrophages than those that received senescent BM‐MSCs with Fc control (Figure 1C , middle), along with a concomitant reduction in the number of remaining senescent GFP + BM‐MSCs (Figure 1C , right), suggesting that DEL‐1 promotes macrophage phagocytosis of senescent BM‐MSCs. To better understand the mechanisms underlying DEL‐1‐mediated macrophage phagocytosis of senescent BM‐MSCs, we set out to examine whether DEL‐1 modulates the expression of surface molecules on senescent BM‐MSCs that could potentially affect their uptake by macrophages. In this regard, the “don't eat me” signal CD47 appears to increase on senescent cells, which can thereby suppress their clearance by macrophages. [ 14 ] However, DEL‐1‐Fc treatment failed to alter CD47 expression on senescent BM‐MSCs as compared to treatment with Fc control (Figure S2 , Supporting Information). We next determined the presence of the “eat me signal” PS on DEL‐1‐Fc‐treated and Fc control‐treated senescent BM‐MSCs by annexin V staining. Flow cytometric analysis showed that DEL‐1‐Fc significantly increased the percentage of annexin V + senescent BM‐MSCs, relative to Fc control (Figure 1D ). In stark contrast, DEL‐1‐Fc had no effect on PS surface abundance when a similar annexin V flow cytometric analysis was performed using healthy, non‐treated BM‐MSCs (Figure 1E ). Given that annexin V staining is indicative of apoptosis, these data suggest that DEL‐1 promotes apoptosis selectively on senescent BM‐MSCs and thus DEL‐1 could have senolytic properties. The senolytic effect of DEL‐1 on senescent BM‐MSCs, as assessed by induction of apoptotic cell death monitored by increased annexin V staining, was reproducible when BM‐MSC senescence was induced by additional stimuli, such as, palbociclib (cyclin D kinase inhibitor) or doxorubicin (genotoxic agent) (Figure S3A,B , Supporting Information, respectively).

Given that DEL‐1 promotes apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSCs, we postulated that the in vivo ability of DEL‐1 to enhance BM‐MSC uptake by macrophages in the TG‐induced peritonitis model (Figure 1C ) may be attributed to its senolytic effect. To address this question, we first determined whether DEL‐1 can induce apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSCs in vivo. Mice were i.p. injected with GFP‐expressing senescent BM‐MSCs together with DEL‐1‐Fc or Fc control. At 3 h post‐injection, the peritoneal contents were aspirated and apoptosis of senescent GFP‐BM‐MSCs was determined by flow cytometric analysis. The presence of DEL‐1‐Fc caused a significant increase in the percentage of annexin V + cells and a concomitant significant decrease in the percentage of annexin V – /7‐AAD – live cells as compared to Fc control (Figure 1F ), suggesting that DEL‐1 induces apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSCs in vivo. Moreover, in vitro, DEL‐1‐Fc decreased the abundance of senescent BM‐MSCs with larger size (Figure S4 , Supporting Information), which may in turn facilitate their phagocytosis by macrophages given that the relatively large size of senescent cells constitutes a natural obstacle to phagocytosis. [ 14 , 43 ]

We next explored whether the ability of DEL‐1 to induce apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSCs is sufficient to promote their clearance by macrophages. To this end, we incubated senescent BM‐MSCs with DEL‐1‐Fc or Fc control for 3 days, and upon washing, the cells were stained with CypHer5E and injected into mice that were subjected to TG‐induced peritonitis 72 h earlier. At 3 h post‐injection (75‐h time point), the peritoneal contents were aspirated and macrophages that phagocytosed senescent BM‐MSCs were identified by flow cytometry as live CD45 + F4/80 + CypHer5E + cells. We observed that the percentage of phagocytic macrophages (CypHer5E + cells in live CD45 + F4/80 + cells) was increased when the senescent BM‐MSCs were pre‐treated, ex vivo , with DEL‐1‐Fc as compared to pretreatment with Fc control (Figure 1G ). A similar experiment was performed in which full‐length DEL‐1‐Fc was replaced by a truncated version of the molecule that contains only the N ‐terminal EGF‐like repeats (designated DEL‐1[E1‐E3]‐Fc) and yielded similar results (Figure 1H ). Moreover, DEL‐1[E1‐E3]‐Fc significantly increased the percentage of annexin V + senescent BM‐MSCs (relative to Fc control), comparably to full‐length DEL‐1‐Fc (Figure 1I ), indicating that the N‐terminal EGF‐like repeats region of DEL‐1 is sufficient to promote the apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSCs and the subsequent clearance thereof by macrophages. Taken together, our findings thus far show conclusively that DEL‐1 promotes macrophage clearance of senescent BM‐MSCs through its senolytic effect.

The second EGF‐like domain of DEL‐1 contains an integrin‐binding RGD motif and many of the known biological functions of DEL‐1 involve interactions with β3 integrin. [ 29 , 34 , 44 ] We thus examined whether the senolytic activity of DEL‐1 is dependent on interaction with β3 integrin expressed by BM‐MSCs, as a first approach to start understanding the underlying mechanism. To this end, we determined whether DEL‐1[RGE]‐Fc, a point‐mutant of DEL‐1 that does not bind β3 integrin due to Glu‐for‐Asp substitution in the RGD motif of DEL‐1, [ 34 , 35 , 37 ] can exert senolytic actions and induce apoptosis in senescent BM‐MSCs. By assessing the activity of caspase‐3/7 as a marker of apoptosis, we showed that DEL‐1[RGE]‐Fc failed to significantly increase caspase‐3/7 activity (relative to Fc control), in contrast to WT DEL‐1‐Fc, which significantly elevated caspase‐3/7 activity (Figure S5A,B , Supporting Information). Moreover, whereas WT DEL‐1‐Fc promoted macrophage phagocytosis of senescent BM‐MSCs in vitro, DEL‐1[RGE]‐Fc failed to promote this function (relative to Fc control) (Figure S5C , Supporting Information). These findings suggest that the integrin‐binding RGD motif of DEL‐1 is required for its senolytic activity. We next investigated potential DEL‐1 receptors on senescent BM‐MSCs involved in apoptosis induction. Given that DEL‐1 can bind the RGD‐recognizing β1 and β3 integrins, which are expressed on MSCs, [ 35 , 45 ] we first tested the ability of DEL‐1 to induce apoptosis in senescent BM‐MSCs that lack β3 integrin. To this end, BM‐MSCs were isolated from mice with MSC‐specific deletion of the β3 integrin gene ( Prx1 Cre+ β3 flox/flox mice). Specific deletion of the β3 integrin‐encoding gene Itgb3 in sorted bone marrow stromal cells from Prx1 Cre+ β3 flox/flox mice was evidenced by a remarkable reduction in Itgb3 integrin mRNA expression by qPCR (Figure S6 , Supporting Information). Although DEL‐1‐Fc induced apoptosis in β3 integrin‐expressing senescent BM‐MSCs, as assessed by annexin V staining and flow cytometric analysis, this effect of DEL‐1‐Fc was abrogated in β3 integrin‐deficient senescent BM‐MSCs ( Figure 2 A ). In contrast, DEL‐1‐Fc retained its ability to induce apoptosis in β3 integrin‐expressing senescent BM‐MSCs that were treated with a neutralizing antibody to β1 integrin (Figure S7 , Supporting Information). Taken together, β3 integrin is required for the senolytic effect of DEL‐1 on senescent BM‐MSCs.

Since β3 integrin mediates DEL‐1‐induced apoptosis and clearance of senescent BM‐MSCs, we assessed β3 integrin expression in various subsets of MSCs in the mouse bone marrow. Flow cytometry revealed that CD73 + MSCs [ 46 ] exhibited the highest expression of β3 integrin compared to other subsets of MSCs in the bone marrow (Figure S8 , Supporting Information), including PDGFRα + Sca1 + (PαS), [ 47 , 48 ] Sca1 + CD29 + , [ 49 ] and LepR + MSCs. [ 50 ] Based on these data and the fact that CD73 (Ecto‐5′‐nucleotidase) regulates the conversion of adenosine monophosphate to adenosine that can induce apoptosis (including in senescent cells) by binding to adenosine receptors, [ 51 , 52 , 53 ] we focused on the expression and function of CD73 on BM‐MSCs for further mechanistic studies.

First, we showed that DEL‐1‐Fc, but not DEL‐1[RGE]‐Fc, significantly increased CD73 expression on senescent BM‐MSCs (Figure 2B ) and, consistently, augmented adenosine concentrations in the culture supernatants of senescent BM‐MSCs (Figure 2C ), as compared to Fc control. To determine whether the senolytic effect of DEL‐1 on senescent BM‐MSCs is dependent on CD73 activity, we used α, β methylene adenosine 5′‐diphosphate (APCP), a specific CD73 inhibitor. Treatment with APCP abrogated DEL‐1‐induced apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSCs (Figure 2D ; Figure S9A , Supporting Information) by restraining adenosine production (Figure 2E ). Furthermore, a pan‐adenosine receptor antagonist blocked DEL‐1‐induced apoptosis (Figure 2F ; Figure S9B , Supporting Information), suggesting that the senolytic effect of DEL‐1 on senescent BM‐MSCs is mediated via the CD73/adenosine/adenosine receptor (AR) pathway. Adenosine was previously shown to promote apoptosis of endothelial cells by inhibiting p38 MAPK activity. [ 54 ] Consistently, p38 MAPK inhibition promotes cisplatin‐induced apoptosis of cancer cells [ 55 ] and the senolytic activity of the SYK inhibitor R406 depends on its ability to inhibit p38 MAPK activity. [ 56 ] To explore whether DEL‐1‐induced apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSC is associated with inhibition of p38 activation, we examined p38 phosphorylation (p‐p38) in senescent BM‐MSCs treated with DEL‐1‐Fc in vitro. DEL‐1‐Fc significantly downregulated the intensity of p‐p38 as compared to Fc control treatment, as shown by flow cytometry (Figure 2G ) and confirmed by western blot analysis (Figure 2H ). Treatment of senescent BM‐MSCs with a pan‐adenosine receptor antagonist abrogated the DEL‐1‐Fc‐induced reduction in p‐p38 (Figure 2I ). Moreover, inhibition of p38 activity in senescent BM‐MSCs using the p38 antagonist SB203580 resulted in dose‐dependent induction of apoptosis (Figure 2J ), thus mimicking the pro‐apoptotic effect of DEL‐1‐Fc (Figure 1D ). BCL‐2 is an anti‐apoptotic molecule and one of the hallmarks of cellular senescence. Targeting the elevated BCL‐2 level in senescent cells with senolytics, such as ABT‐263 and ABT‐ 737, is a potential strategy for eliminating senescent cells. [ 18 , 26 ] To determine if BCL‐2 is a downstream target of p38 inhibition‐mediated apoptosis in senescent BM‐MSCs, we assessed its expression following DEL‐1 treatment. Intriguingly, we observed that DEL‐1 significantly decreased the expression of BCL‐2 in senescent BM‐MSCs, at both the mRNA and protein level, as assessed by quantitative PCR and flow cytometry, respectively (Figure 2K,L ). Furthermore, the expression of other anti‐apoptotic BCL‐2 family members, B‐cell lymphoma‐extra large (BCL‐XL) and myeloid cell leukemia‐1 (MCL‐1), was also significantly diminished by DEL‐1 treatment (Figure S10 , Supporting Information). Subsequently, flow cytometric analysis showed that BCL‐2 expression was inhibited by the p38 inhibitor, SB203580 in a dose‐dependent manner (Figure 2M ), indicating that BCL‐2 is a downstream target of p38. Importantly, a pan‐adenosine receptor antagonist abrogated the DEL‐1‐mediated inhibition of BCL‐2 expression (Figure 2N ). Taken together, our findings suggest that DEL‐1 binds β3 integrin on senescent BM‐MSCs and promotes their apoptosis via a CD73/adenosine receptor/p38 MAPK/BCL‐2 pathway (Figure S11 , Supporting Information).

To investigate whether DEL‐1 exerts senolytic action also in vivo and understand the underlying mechanisms, we employed a doxorubicin‐induced senescence and bone loss model [ 24 ] in DEL‐1‐deficient ( Del1 KO ) mice and WT littermate controls. Doxorubicin, a potent inducer of DNA damage, [ 57 , 58 ] triggers cellular senescence (including in stromal cells) and the accompanying SASP, thereby leading to bone loss that is counteracted by senescent cell clearance. [ 24 ] Del1 KO and WT mice were administered a biologically relevant dose of doxorubicin (5 mg kg −1 , body weight) [ 59 ] once a week for 4 consecutive weeks ( Figure 3 A ). This allowed us to examine cellular senescence and associated gene expression in the bone marrow as well as bone mass. Microcomputed tomography (µCT) imaging revealed significant femoral bone loss in both the cortical and trabecular compartments in Del1 KO mice as compared to WT controls. We observed that the cortical thickness (Ct.Th) in the mid‐diaphysis in De1 KO mice was significantly lower than in WT mice (Figure 3B ). In the trabecular compartment, Del1 KO mice displayed decreased trabecular volume fraction (Tb.BV/TV), trabecular number (Tb.N), thickness (Tb.Th), but increased separation (Tb.Sp), as compared to WT control (Figure 3C ). Given our previously published observations that Del1 KO mice and WT littermate controls have comparable bone densities (in the femur and spine) under steady‐state conditions ( i.e ., without inflammatory or other challenge), [ 33 ] the exacerbated bone loss observed in doxorubicin‐treated Del1 KO mice (relative to WT littermates) is likely attributed exclusively to the doxorubicin challenge.

Next, we determined whether the increased bone loss in DEL‐1 deficiency results from reduced bone formation and/or enhanced bone resorption. To this end, we used ELISA to measure the serum levels of osteocalcin, as a marker of bone formation, as well as the serum levels collagen type I cross‐linked C‐telopeptide (CTX1) and tartrate‐resistant acid phosphatase 5b (TRAcP 5b), both being markers of bone resorption. In comparison to WT controls, Del1 KO mice exhibited reduced osteocalcin concentrations (Figure 3D ) and increased concentrations of CTX1 and TRAcP 5b (Figure 3E ), consistent with osteocalcin and TRAP staining, respectively, as shown in Figure 3F .

Moreover, qPCR analysis indicated a significant increase in the expression of the senescence‐related genes p21 and p53 (but not of p16 in the bone marrow of Del‐1 KO mice as compared to WT mice (Figure 3G ). Among SASP genes investigated in the same assay, Cxcl2 was significantly upregulated in Del1 KO mice, whereas a trend for increased expression of Il6 and Tgfβ1 did not reach statistical significance (Figure 3G ). This increase in SASP was further confirmed at the protein level, as TGFβ1 and CXCL2 concentrations were significantly elevated in the bone marrow fluid of Del‐1 KO mice (Figure 3H ). Moreover, histological analysis revealed an abundance of p21 + cells in the bone marrow compartment of Del1 KO mice (Figure 3I ). These findings underscore the ability of endogenous DEL‐1 to prevent senescence‐associated bone loss while downregulating the expression of key senescent markers in the bone marrow.

Given that CD45 – CD31 – stromal cells are the primary targets of doxorubicin‐induced senescence, [ 24 ] we examined various subsets of MSC populations, including PDGFRα + Sca1 + CD45 – CD31 – Ter119 – (PαS), Sca1 + CD29 + CD45 – CD31 – Ter119 – , and CD73 + CD45 – CD31 – Ter119 – cells in the bone marrow post‐doxorubicin treatment. Whereas no difference was observed between WT and Del1 KO mice with regard to the numbers of PαS and Sca1 + CD29 + MSCs (Figure S12 , Supporting Information), we observed a substantial increase in the number of CD73 + stromal cells in the bone marrow of Del1 KO mice, as compared to WT littermates, at day 7 following a single dose of doxorubicin (10 mg kg −1 ) ( Figure 4 A ) and at day 28 following doxorubicin treatment (5 mg kg −1 ) once weekly for 4 weeks (Figure 4A , right). This increase in the numbers of CD73 + stromal cells in DEL‐1 deficiency was not observed in the absence of doxorubicin treatment (data not shown). Further characterization of CD73 + bone marrow stromal cells revealed that this subset had a higher frequency of γH 2 AX expression (marker of DNA damage [ 60 ] ) in Del1 KO than in WT mice (Figure 4B ), along with reduced percentage of Ki67‐positive (proliferative) cells (Figure 4C ), indicating a heightened senescent phenotype of these cells under the condition of in vivo DEL‐1 deficiency. These findings suggest that DEL‐1 deficiency promotes senescence selectively in the CD73 + MSCs population and leads to their accumulation in the bone marrow after doxorubicin administration. Consistently, live CD73 + CD45 – CD31 – Ter119 – MSCs from Del1 KO mice displayed increased expression of senescence‐related genes ( p21, Il6, Cxcl2 ) (Figure 4D ) and decreased annexin V‐determined apoptosis (Figure 4E ), as compared to WT controls at day 7 following doxorubicin treatment. At the same time point, moreover, the bone marrow fluid of Del1 KO mice contained decreased concentration of adenosine (relative to WT controls; Figure 4F ), a key component of the DEL‐1‐induced pro‐apoptotic pathway in senescent BM‐MSCs (Figure 2 ; Figure S11 , Supporting Information). Consistent with the importance of β3 integrin in mediating DEL‐1‐induced apoptosis that proceeds via a CD73/adenosine pathway (Figure 2 ; Figure S11 , Supporting Information), we showed that β3 integrin expression was significantly higher in CD73 + PαS than in CD73 – PαS MSCs (Figure S13 , Supporting Information). Consistently moreover, DEL‐1 deficiency resulted in increased frequency of γH 2 AX + cells selectively within the CD73 + PαS population (Figure 4G ), since γH 2 AX expression in CD73 – PαS cells was not affected by the presence or absence of DEL‐1 (Figure 4H ), indicating an increased senescent phenotype in the β3 integrin‐rich CD73 + PαS population. This was confirmed by subsequent analyses demonstrating an increased frequency of p21 + cells in the CD73 + PαS population (Figure 4I ), but not in the CD73 – PαS population (Figure 4J ) in DEL‐1‐deficient mice.

These in vivo data are consistent with the in vitro dissected mechanism of the DEL‐1 senolytic action and collectively suggest that β3 integrin‐expressing CD73 + senescent MSCs accumulate in the DEL‐1‐deficient bone marrow. At least in part, this is attributed to reduced apoptosis and hence impaired senolytic clearance of CD73 + senescent MSCs in DEL‐1 deficiency, which would otherwise occur in the presence of DEL‐1.

We next determined the cellular source of DEL‐1 responsible for its senolytic effect on senescent MSCs in the bone marrow. Based on the bone marrow expression profile of DEL‐1, [ 34 ] we reasoned that DEL‐1 could be derived from endothelial cells and/or from MSCs. By crossing Del1 flox/flox with VE‐Cad Cre+ or Prx1 Cre+ mice, we generated mice with specific deletion of DEL‐1 in vascular endothelial cells or in MSCs, respectively. Specific deletion of the DEL‐1‐encoding Edil3 gene in sorted bone marrow stromal cells from Prx1 Cre+ Del1 flox/flox mice ( Del1 MSCKO ) and in sorted lung endothelial cells from VE‐ Cad Cre+ Del1 flox/flox mice ( Del1 ECKO ) was suggested by the strongly reduced Edil3 mRNA expression by qPCR (Figure S14 , Supporting Information). We first administered doxorubicin to both VE‐ Cad Cre+ Del1 flox/flox mice ( Del1 ECKO ) and VE‐ Cad Cre– Del1 flox/flox controls ( Del1 ECWT ) and examined the number of senescent CD73 + PαS MSCs in the bone marrow at day 7. Strikingly, the absence of DEL‐1 from endothelial cells resulted in a significant increase in the number of senescent MSCs (p21 + CD73 + PαS or C 12 FDG + CD73 + PαS) in the bone marrow ( Figure 5 A,B ). In contrast, no discernible difference was observed in the number of senescent CD73 + PαS MSCs in the bone marrow of Prx1 Cre+ Del1 flox/flox ( Del1 MSCKO ) and Prx1 Cre– Del1 flox/flox ( Del1 MSCWT ) mice (Figure S15 , Supporting Information). These results suggest that endothelial cells are a major cellular source of DEL‐1 responsible for its senolytic activity on senescent MSCs in the bone marrow of doxorubicin‐treated mice, implying that secreted DEL‐1 acts in a paracrine manner (Figure S11 , Supporting Information).

To further corroborate the importance of endothelial DEL‐1 in promoting apoptosis of senescent MSCs in the doxorubicin‐induced bone loss model, we employed mice with endothelial cell‐specific overexpression of DEL‐1 (EC‐Del1 mice). [ 29 , 38 , 61 ] Microcomputed tomography analysis revealed a significant increase in trabecular volume fraction (Tb.BV/TV), trabecular number (Tb.N), trabecular thickness (Tb.Th) and a decrease in trabecular separation (Tb.Sp) in EC‐Del1 mice compared to WT mice (Figure 5D ), whereas there was no significant difference between the two groups with regard to cortical thickness (Ct.Th) (Figure 5C ). This bone‐protective effect was associated with a significant reduction in the number of senescent p21 + CD73 + PαS or C 12 FDG + CD73 + PαS MSCs in the bone marrow of EC‐Del1 mice as compared to WT littermates (Figure 5E,F ). In contrast, no difference was observed in the numbers of CD73‐negative senescent MSCs (p21 + CD73 – PαS cells or C 12 FDG + CD73 – PαS cells) between WT and EC‐Del1 mice (Figure 5G ; Figure S16 , Supporting Information), substantiating our earlier findings that DEL‐1 selectively targets CD73‐positive senescent MSCs (Figure 5E–G ; Figure S16 , Supporting Information). Importantly, the percentage of apoptotic (caspase‐3‐positive) cells in senescent p21 + CD73 + PαS MSCs was significantly enhanced in the bone marrow of EC‐Del1 mice as compared to WT littermates (Figure 5H ). In contrast, no such difference in the frequency of caspase‐3‐positive cells in p21 – CD73 + PαS MSCs cells was observed (Figure 5I ), indicating that DEL‐1 selectively promotes apoptosis in senescent MSCs, as we also showed in vitro (Figure 1D,E ).

Whereas CD73 is important for the senolytic activity of DEL‐1 in vitro (Figure 2 ), such a requirement has not been addressed yet in vivo. To determine the role of CD73 in the senolytic effect mediated by DEL‐1 on senescent MSCs in the doxorubicin‐induced bone loss model, we employed CD73‐deficient ( Cd73 KO ) mice and mice with endothelial‐specific overexpression of DEL‐1 in the CD73‐deficient background ( Cd73 KO /EC‐Del1 mice), which we generated by crossing Cd73 KO mice and EC‐Del1 mice. As expected from our earlier experiment (Figure 5E,F ), 7 days after doxorubicin administration, there was a significant reduction in the number of senescent MSCs (p21 + PαS or C 12 FDG + PαS) in the bone marrow of EC‐Del1 mice, as compared to their WT littermates (Figure 5J,K ). In contrast, in the CD73‐deficient background, the endothelial cell‐specific overexpression of DEL‐1 had no effect on the number of senescent PαS cells (p21 + PαS or C 12 FDG + PαS), since the numbers of senescent PαS cells were comparable between the bone marrow of Cd73 KO and Cd73 KO /EC‐Del1 mice (Figure 5L,M ). Furthermore, no difference in doxorubicin‐mediated bone mass was observed between WT and EC‐Del1 mice in Cd73 KO background (Figure S17 , Supporting Information). Taken together, these findings demonstrate that endothelial cell‐derived DEL‐1 mediates bone protection and clearance of senescent MSCs in a CD73‐depenent manner during chemotherapy‐induced senescence‐associated bone loss.

Aging‐related cellular senescence has been established as a major contributing factor to bone loss in old mice, reminiscent of osteoporosis in elderly humans. [ 62 ] DEL‐1 expression is diminished in mucosal tissue in old age in both mice and humans. [ 33 , 63 ] Correspondingly, we observed a significant reduction (>60%) in DEL‐1 expression in the bone marrow of aged mice (22‐month‐old) as compared to their younger counterparts (3‐month‐old) ( Figure 6 A , left). Conversely, the gene expression of the senescence‐associated genes p21 and p53 were found to be significantly higher in the bone marrow of aged mice as compared to their young counterparts (Figure 6A , middle and right). Consistently, we observed that the numbers of CD73 + PαS MSCs (Figure S18 , Supporting Information, left) and senescent p21 + CD73 + MSCs (Figure 6B ) exhibited a significant increase in the bone marrow of aged mice (21‐month‐old) compared to young mice (2‐month‐old). Therefore, there is a reverse relationship between MSC senescence and DEL‐1 expression in the bone marrow microenvironment.

Further investigations revealed that 22‐month‐old Del1 KO mice displayed a decrease in cortical thickness of the femur and notable damage in trabecular bone microarchitecture, as opposed to age‐matched WT littermate controls (Figure 6C,D ). Consistent with doxorubicin‐induced bone loss, TRAP and osteocalcin immunostaining suggested the presence of increased osteoclasts and reduced osteoblasts (Figure S19 , Supporting Information). Moreover, in their bone marrow, 22‐month‐old Del1 KO mice displayed elevated mRNA expression of p21, p53, Il6, Cxcl1, and Tgfβ1 (Figure 6E ) as well as increased numbers of senescent p21 + CD73 + PαS cells (Figure 6F ) when compared to WT littermates. In contrast, the numbers of senescent p21 + CD73 – PαS cells were comparable between 22‐month‐old WT and Del1 KO mice (Figure 6G ). Conversely, but consistently, 22‐23‐month‐old EC‐Del1 mice exhibited a significant reduction in the number of senescent p21 + CD73 + PαS, as well C 12 FDG + CD73 + PαS, cell populations relative to WT littermates (Figure 6J,K ), accompanied by an increase in trabecular bone microarchitectural parameters (Figure 6I ). In contrast, no significant difference was observed in cortical bone thickness (Figure 6H ). In a subsequent TRAP and osteocalcin immunostaining analysis, we observed that EC‐Del1 mice exhibited overall increased bone formation (Figure S20 , Supporting Information). These findings from an aging‐driven bone marrow senescence model reinforce the notion derived from the chemotherapy‐induced senescence model that the senolytic action of DEL‐1 targets a specific (CD73‐positive) subset of senescent PαS MSCs.

Senescent cells also accumulate in the periodontal tissues in old age and are thought to exacerbate local inflammation as well as tissue destruction including alveolar bone loss, in part through the release of SASP proteins. [ 64 , 65 , 66 ] In aged mice, senescent cells are particularly abundant in the periodontal ligament (PDL), the structure that connects the root of the tooth to the alveolar bone. [ 65 ] The PDL is of central importance to the inflammatory mechanisms that drive bone loss in periodontitis [ 65 , 67 , 68 ] but is also a rich source of MSCs that are responsible for periodontal soft tissue and bone regeneration. [ 69 , 70 , 71 , 72 ] We determined whether local administration of DEL‐1‐Fc (or Fc control) or systemic administration of erythromycin (ERM), a macrolide antibiotic which upregulates periodontal tissue expression of DEL‐1, [ 73 ] can reduce the number of senescent cells within the PDL space of aged mice. To this end, we used an aging model of naturally occurring periodontitis. [ 74 ] As a negative (vehicle) control for systemic administration, we used ethanol (EtOH), and for a positive control we used Bis‐2‐(5‐phenylacetamido‐1,3,4‐thiadiazol‐2‐yl)ethyl sulfide (BPTES), a selective inhibitor of glutaminase‐1, which causes senolysis and attenuates aging‐related organ dysfunction. [ 75 ] 18‐month‐old mice were treated with the above mentioned experimental and control treatments for 9 days, based on our recent study where systemic administration of ERM promoted alveolar bone regeneration in mice of the same age within 9 days, in a manner dependent on DEL‐1 upregulation. [ 76 ] Nine days post‐treatment, we performed SA‐β‐gal staining on maxillary sections to quantify senescent (SA‐β‐gal + ) cells within the PDL space. Senescent cells were readily detected in the PDL space of untreated Fc control‐treated old mice but not in untreated young mice ( Figure 7 A ). The number of SA‐β‐gal + cells, however, were significantly decreased in mice treated with DEL‐1‐Fc, ERM or BPTES (Figure 7A,B ). Similar results were obtained when immunofluorescence histochemistry was used to quantify the numbers of p16 + (Figure 7C , top) and p21 + cells (Figure 7C , bottom) within the PDL space of treated and control aged mice. Specifically, the numbers of cells identified by these two senescent markers were significantly reduced by DEL‐1‐Fc, ERM or BPTES (Figure 7C,D ). Furthermore, evaluation of mRNA expression of p16 and p21 by PDL cells isolated from the various treated and control groups of mice was consistent with the microscopic analysis; indeed, treatments with DEL‐1‐Fc, ERM or BPTES caused a significant decrease in p16 and p21 mRNA levels in aged mouse PDL cells (Figure 7E ). The same experimental treatments ( i.e ., DEL‐1‐Fc, ERM and BPTES) also resulted in bone regeneration relative to the negative controls (Fc or EtOH) (Figure 7F ), indicating that a reduction in the number of senescent cells in the PDL (Figure 7A–E ) is associated with reversal of bone loss. Moreover, we have shown that in aged periodontal tissues, ERM administration enhanced the clearance of terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL)‐positive cells, while concurrently reducing p21 levels. The combined decrease in p21 and enhanced apoptotic cell clearance suggests that ERM promotes the elimination of senescent cells in the mesenchymal stromal cell‐rich periodontal ligament (Figure S21 , Supporting Information). These findings align with the role of DEL‐1 in modulating senescence‐associated pathways in periodontal tissue, as seen in the femoral bone.

sections.discussion:
While the emergence of extrinsic senolytic drugs shows promise in preventing senescence and revitalizing aged tissues, [ 77 , 78 ] the precise endogenous mechanism(s) through which the local tissue microenvironment controls the survival and buildup of senescent cells remains incompletely understood. Here, we present evidence that DEL‐1 serves as an endogenous senolytic protein, which effectively promotes the apoptosis of senescent MSCs in the bone marrow and prevents bone loss, as shown in three independent senescence‐associated bone loss models. The fact that the expression of DEL‐1 declines gradually with increasing age [ 33 , 79 ] suggests that this endogenous senolytic mechanism is progressively compromised, thereby further accelerating the accumulation of senescent cells. To the best of our knowledge, no other endogenous protein with senolytic properties has been previously described.

Mechanistically, the senolytic action of DEL‐1 was shown to be dependent on β3 integrin, one of its known cellular receptors, [ 28 ] and the ecto‐5′‐nucleotidase CD73, the expression of which is upregulated by DEL‐1. The expression and functional significance of CD73 in senescent MSCs in the bone marrow has remained largely unexplored. Here we showed that DEL‐1 increases the levels of adenosine in the culture supernatants of senescent BM‐MSCs, in a CD73‐dependent manner, leading to their apoptosis. Indeed, inhibiting CD73 or adenosine receptors effectively blocked DEL‐1‐induced apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSCs, which also involved attenuation of p38 MAPK activity and downstream reduction in BCL‐2 expression, ultimately leading to apoptosis (see model in Figure S11 , Supporting Information).

Consistently, we noted an inverse correlation between MSC senescence and DEL‐1 expression within the bone marrow of aged mice as well as mice subjected to chemotherapy. For instance, deficiency in DEL‐1 contributed to heightened BM‐MSC senescence in both the aging‐ and chemotherapy‐induced senescence models. Endothelial (but not MSC)‐specific deficiency of DEL‐1 resulted in higher BM‐MSC senescence, implying that endothelial‐derived secreted DEL‐1 acts as a paracrine senolytic factor (Figure S11 , Supporting Information). Consistently, the overexpression of DEL‐1 in endothelial cells mitigated cellular senescence in the bone marrow. These observations underscore the pivotal role of endothelium‐derived DEL‐1 as a key regulator of MSC senescence in the bone marrow.

In line with the critical importance of a CD73/adenosine pathway in mediating DEL‐1‐induced apoptosis of senescent cells, DEL‐1 was shown to selectively target CD73‐positive senescent MSCs, namely the CD73 + PαS stromal cells in the bone marrow, in two different in vivo models (chemotherapy‐induced and aging‐induced senescence). CD73 + PαS MSCs exhibit elevated expression of β3 integrin in comparison to other subsets of BM‐MSCs, including Sca1 + CD29 + MSCs, CD73 – PαS, and LepR + MSCs. This explains, at least in part, why the β3 integrin‐mediated senolytic action of DEL‐1 preferentially targets senescent CD73 + PαS MSCs. Importantly, a recent investigation has shown that CD73 + MSCs exhibit heightened proliferative activity and a superior capacity for osteogenic differentiation, thereby promoting bone regeneration more effectively than CD73 – MSCs. [ 46 ] This finding implies that the accumulation of senescent CD73 + MSCs in the bone marrow may lead to severe impairment of bone homeostasis.

Of note, in the bone microenvironment, the CD73 + MSCs exhibit a distinct perivascular distribution. [ 46 ] This localization is particularly intriguing, given that DEL‐1 is also prominently localized in the perivascular area in the bone marrow, [ 34 ] suggesting a potential close interaction between DEL‐1 and CD73 + MSCs. Consistently, we found that vascular endothelial overexpression of DEL‐1 had a pronounced effect on the regulation of the senescent CD73 + PαS (but not of CD73 – PαS) MSC numbers in the bone marrow. Our current study therefore implicates CD73 + PαS + MSCs as major targets of endothelial DEL‐1‐mediated senolysis and explains why this subset can accumulate in old age, when the bone marrow levels of DEL‐1 decline severely.

Previously, we showed that DEL‐1 binds to PS through its discoidin I‐like domains, thereby enabling the recognition of apoptotic cells. [ 29 ] Moreover, the concomitant interaction of DEL‐1 with β3 integrin on macrophages, through an RGD motif in its second EGF‐like repeat, promotes the efferocytosis of apoptotic cells. In the present study, DEL‐1 was shown to depend on its RGD motif and on β3 integrin expression in order to induce apoptosis of senescent BM‐MSCs and thereby promote their phagocytosis by macrophages. In particular, a truncated version of DEL‐1 containing the N ‐terminal EGF‐like repeats region but lacking the discoidin I‐like domains was sufficient to reproduce the senolytic effect of the parent molecule. This finding suggests that the senolytic effect of DEL‐1 is distinct from its efferocytosis‐promoting effect.

Our present work also revealed that DEL‐1 inhibited the activation/phosphorylation of p38 MAPK and expression of BCL‐2, thereby promoting apoptosis in senescent BM‐MSCs. This finding aligns with the mechanism of action of the senolytic agent R406 (SYK inhibitor), which exerts its senolytic effect through dual inhibition of FAK and p38 MAPK. [ 56 ] Inhibition of p38 MAPK in our senescent BM‐MSC model caused apoptosis, in agreement with an earlier study where p38 MAPK inhibition promoted tumor apoptosis. [ 55 ] It should be noted, however, that the activation of p38 MAPK can exhibit either pro‐ or anti‐apoptotic effects, depending on the specific cellular environment. [ 80 , 81 , 82 , 83 ] Several established senolytic agents directly target anti‐apoptotic BCL‐2 family proteins, including ABT‐263, ABT‐737, and ABT‐199. [ 17 , 18 , 84 ] Importantly, we demonstrated that DEL‐1 inhibits p‐p38 MAPK, leading to a reduction in BCL‐2 levels, indicating BCL‐2 acts downstream of p‐p38 MAPK to regulate apoptosis, consistent with previous findings. [ 85 ] The downregulation of BCL‐2, a key anti‐apoptotic protein and hallmark of cellular senescence, lowers the apoptotic resistance threshold in senescent cells and appears to be a critical mediator of DEL‐1‐induced senolysis.

Senescent osteogenic progenitors, including MSCs, play a crucial role in driving skeletal senescence and bone loss. [ 27 , 41 ] However, the extent to which the elimination of senescent MSCs can prevent senescence‐induced or age‐related bone loss remains incompletely understood. Recent studies suggest that senescent MSCs also affect bone formation. [ 26 , 27 , 86 ] Notably, increased miR‐29 expression has been observed in senescent MSCs, and targeting miR‐29a in these cells impedes skeletal senescence and enhances bone mass by promoting osteoblast bone‐forming activity. [ 86 ] Furthermore, senolytic agents have been shown to boost osteogenic activity of aged, but not young, BM‐MSCs in vitro and in vivo, suggesting that the removal of senescent BM‐MSCs enhances bone‐forming potential. [ 26 ] Additionally, targeting senescent BM‐MSCs by treatment of quercetin efficiently eliminates senescent cells in bone, restores the function of BM‐MSCs, and promotes bone formation in aged mouse models. [ 27 ] Consistent with these findings, doxorubicin‐challenged Del1 KO mice displayed decreased concentrations of osteocalcin (a marker of bone formation) and increased concentrations of CTX1 and TRAcP 5b (markers of bone resorption), along with osteocalcin and TRAP immunostaining, suggesting that both impaired bone formation and elevated bone resorption contributed to their aggravated bone loss as compared to their DEL‐1‐sufficient littermate controls. Stated another way, the treatment with DEL‐1 mitigates doxorubicin‐induced bone loss by promoting both bone formation and inhibiting bone resorption.

Given that DEL‐1 mediates its senolytic effect in a β3 integrin‐dependent manner and recent findings that β3 integrin is significantly elevated in senescent cells and aged tissues, [ 87 ] we can infer that DEL‐1 can preferentially target senescent, rather than healthy, MSCs. Although DEL‐1 cannot specifically identify senescent MSCs (healthy cells may also express β3 integrin), healthy cells are not susceptible to the apoptosis‐inducing effect of DEL‐1, as shown in the present study. Therefore, by targeting β3 integrin‐expressing cells, DEL‐1 can efficiently exert a beneficial action (senolysis) without potential adverse effects on healthy cells.

Interestingly, even a relatively modest proportion (≈10–15%) of senescent cells in old primates can lead to significant tissue dysfunction. [ 88 ] The hereby established senolytic effect of DEL‐1 renders this protein a promising therapeutic approach to counteract cellular senescence and its pathologic sequalae. In this regard, administration of endogenous proteins as replacement therapies (due to aging‐related decline in their expression as is the case with DEL‐1) are likely to exhibit minor, if any, potential safety issues and have increased probability of FDA approval as compared with extrinsic biologics. [ 89 , 90 , 91 ] Moreover, expression of DEL‐1 in old age can be reinstated by administration of DEL‐1‐inducing agents such as macrolide antibiotics, including synthetic derivatives free of antibiotic action. [ 76 ] Given our present findings that endothelial cells constitute a major cellular source of DEL‐1 that is responsible for its senolytic effect, it is of particular significance to note that macrolides were also shown to upregulate the expression of DEL‐1 in human endothelial cells. [ 73 ] As a proof‐of‐concept, here we showed that local administration of DEL‐1 or systemic administration of a macrolide (ERM) reduced the numbers of senescent cells within the PDL space of aged mice, which are known to express very low levels of DEL‐1 mRNA and protein. [ 33 , 76 ] Although the ability of DEL‐1 and ERM to reverse bone loss in aged mice was also shown in our previous publication, we did not previously implicate senolysis as a contributing mechanism. [ 76 ] Importantly, in our present work the senolytic and bone protective effects of DEL‐1 and ERM were comparable to those of BPTES, an established senolytic that ameliorates senescence‐associated pathology in different organs. [ 75 ]

In summary, our comprehensive findings establish DEL‐1 as a novel endogenously expressed senolytic protein, which promotes the removal of accumulated senescent MSCs in the bone marrow, particularly the CD73 + PαS stromal cell subset, as shown using both chemotherapy‐induced and aging‐related cellular senescence models. Moreover, DEL‐1 caused a reduction of senescent cells in the periphery, where its senolytic activity was associated with reversal of aging‐related periodontal bone loss. Senolytic drugs have limitations in effectively eliminating senescent cells due to the dynamic and highly heterogeneous nature of various senescence programs. This results in different types of senescent cells showing varying levels of sensitivity to current senolytic treatments. [ 92 , 93 , 94 ] To overcome these challenges and advance anti‐aging interventions, there is a strong demand for the development of new approaches that can selectively target and remove senescent cells in various cell types and tissues. In this regard, DEL‐1 displays selectivity for senescent CD73 + PαS stem cells, which in the bone marrow express high levels of the DEL‐1 receptor β3‐integrin. Thus, our findings may provide a potential strategy to enhance the senolytic efficacy against a specific subset of senescent MSCs, which promote loss of skeletal bone in old age and other contexts such as chemotherapy.
